name: False Cognates (French-English)
moduleIntroduction:
Welcome! This module helps you avoid common mistakes with **false cognates** - words that look similar in French and English but have different meanings.

False cognates (or 'faux amis' in French) can cause embarrassing misunderstandings. For example, the French word 'actuellement' looks like the English 'actually', but they mean very different things!

In this module, you'll learn 50+ false cognate pairs that commonly confuse Francophone learners. Each lesson provides:
• The English word and its real meaning
• The French word it resembles
• Common mistakes and how to avoid them
• Memory tricks to help you remember

Mastering these false cognates will make your English more accurate and prevent common errors in professional and academic situations.
contrastiveExplanation:
False cognates are words that look or sound similar in two languages but have different meanings. They're especially tricky for French speakers learning English because:

**1. Actually vs. Actuellement**
• French 'actuellement' = currently, at present
• English 'actually' = in fact, really
• Error: 'I am actually working' (meaning 'currently') ❌
• Correct: 'I am currently working' ✅

**2. Assist vs. Assister**
• French 'assister à' = to attend
• English 'assist' = to help
• Error: 'I will assist the meeting' ❌
• Correct: 'I will attend the meeting' ✅

**3. Library vs. Librairie**
• French 'librairie' = bookstore (buy books)
• English 'library' = bibliothèque (borrow books)
• Error: 'I bought books at the library' ❌
• Correct: 'I bought books at the bookstore' ✅

**4. Demand vs. Demander**
• French 'demander' = to ask (polite)
• English 'demand' = to insist strongly (forceful)
• Error: 'Can I demand you a question?' ❌
• Correct: 'Can I ask you a question?' ✅

**5. Sensible vs. Sensible**
• French 'sensible' = sensitive (emotional)
• English 'sensible' = practical, reasonable
• Error: 'He is very sensible to criticism' ❌
• Correct: 'He is very sensitive to criticism' ✅

These false cognates span all areas of life - work, school, health, shopping, and daily conversation. Learning them will significantly improve your English accuracy.

commonErrors.wrong: I am actually working at the ministry.
commonErrors.correct: I am currently working at the ministry.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: 'Actuellement' means 'currently', not 'actually'. Use 'currently' for 'actuellement' and 'actually' for 'en fait'.

commonErrors.wrong: I will assist the meeting tomorrow.
commonErrors.correct: I will attend the meeting tomorrow.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: 'Assister à' means 'to attend'. Use 'assist' only when you mean 'to help someone'.

commonErrors.wrong: I bought my textbooks at the library.
commonErrors.correct: I bought my textbooks at the bookstore.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: 'Librairie' is where you buy books. 'Library' is 'bibliothèque' where you borrow books for free.

commonErrors.wrong: Can I demand you a question?
commonErrors.correct: Can I ask you a question?
commonErrors.frenchConnection: 'Demander' is to ask politely. 'Demand' is forceful and strong, like 'exiger'.

commonErrors.wrong: I will eventually come to the party.
commonErrors.correct: I will possibly come to the party.

items.questionText: "Where do you work?" "I ___ work at the Ministry of Education."
items.feedback: Correct! To express 'actuellement' in French (meaning 'at present'), use 'currently' in English. 'Actually' means 'en fait' (in fact), used to correct or emphasize truth. Example: 'Actually, I prefer tea, not coffee.'

falseCognate.englishMeaning: in fact, really (used to correct or emphasize)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am actually working' when you mean 'I am currently working'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Actually = En fait (In fact) | Currently = Actuellement (At present)

items.questionText: "Will you ___ the conference at the university tomorrow?"
items.feedback: Perfect! To be present at a meeting or event, use 'attend' (assister à). 'Assist' means 'to help someone' (aider). Example: 'The nurse will assist the doctor' (help), but 'I will attend the meeting' (be present).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to help, give support to
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I will assist the meeting' when you mean 'attend'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Assist = Aider (to help) | Attend = Assister à (to be present)

items.questionText: "I am ___ for my friend at the motor park."
items.feedback: Correct! The verb 'attendre' in French means 'to wait (for)' in English. 'Attend' means 'to be present at' (assister à). Example: 'I attend school' (I go to school), but 'I am waiting for my friend' (j'attends mon ami).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to be present at, to go to
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am attending my friend' when you mean 'waiting for'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Attend = Assister à (be present) | Wait for = Attendre

items.questionText: "I need to go to the ___ to buy my textbooks for school."
items.feedback: Excellent! A 'librairie' in French is a 'bookstore' in English (where you BUY books). A 'library' is a 'bibliothèque' where you BORROW books for free. Memory trick: Library = Borrow, Bookstore = Buy.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: bookstore (a shop where you buy books)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: bibliothèque (a place to borrow books for free)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I bought books at the library' when you mean 'bookstore'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Library = Bibliothèque (Borrow) | Bookstore = Librairie (Buy)

items.questionText: "The conference will have over 200 teachers from across Cameroon." What is being described?
options: A single lecture by one professor
A large multi-day event with many speakers
items.correctAnswer: A large multi-day event with many speakers
items.feedback: Correct! A 'conference' in English is a large, multi-day event with many speakers (un congrès or colloque). A single academic talk is a 'lecture' or 'presentation'. 'Conférence' in French often means a single lecture.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: a lecture, academic talk, or press conference
falseCognate.englishMeaning: a large, multi-day meeting with many speakers
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am going to the conference hall' when you mean a single lecture
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Conference = Big multi-day event (congrès) | Lecture = Single talk (conférence)

items.questionText: "Please let me ___ you to the Headmaster, Mr. Njoya."
items.feedback: Perfect! Use 'introduce' when presenting one person to another (présenter). 'Introduire' in French means 'to insert' or 'to put inside'. Example: 'He inserted the key' (Il a introduit la clé), but 'Let me introduce you' (présenter).

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to insert, to put inside, to bring in
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to present one person to another
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'He introduced the USB key' when you mean 'inserted'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Introduce = Présenter (people) | Insert = Introduire (objects)

items.questionText: "I ___ go to Kribi this weekend, but I'm not sure yet."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Éventuellement' means 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. 'Eventually' means 'finally' or 'in the end' after a long time. Example: 'If you study hard, you will eventually pass' (finalement).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: in the end, finally (after a long time)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I will eventually come' when you mean 'possibly'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Eventually = Finalement (Finally) | Possibly = Éventuellement

items.questionText: "Be careful what you say to him; he is very ___ to criticism."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Sensible' in French means 'sensitive' (emotional). But in English, 'sensible' means 'practical' or 'reasonable' (raisonnable). Use 'sensitive' for emotions. Example: 'It is sensible to save money' (practical).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: practical, reasonable (having good judgment)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'He is very sensible' when you mean 'sensitive'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Sensible = Raisonnable (Practical) | Sensitive = Sensible (Emotional)

items.questionText: "My bad exam results ___ my parents very much."
items.feedback: That's right! 'Décevoir' means 'to disappoint'. 'Deceive' means 'to trick' or 'to lie to' (tromper). Example: 'The seller deceived me' (he tricked me), but 'I disappointed my teacher' (I let them down).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to trick, to lie to
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I deceived my teacher' when you mean 'disappointed'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Deceive = Tromper (to trick) | Disappoint = Décevoir

items.questionText: "Excuse me, may I ___ you a question about the assignment?"
items.feedback: That's right! Use 'ask' for polite requests (demander). 'Demand' is very strong and forceful (exiger), like when workers demand higher pay. 'Ask' is polite, 'demand' is aggressive.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to insist strongly (forceful, often impolite)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'Can I demand you something?' when you mean 'ask'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Demand = Exiger (to insist) | Ask = Demander (polite)

items.questionText: "The ___ from Yaoundé to Bamenda takes many hours by bus."
items.feedback: Excellent! A 'journey' is a trip (voyage). 'Journée' in French means 'day'. Example: 'Bonne journée!' = 'Have a good day!' (not 'good journey'). 'Journey' is for travel.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a trip (the act of traveling)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I had a long journey' when you mean 'a long day'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Journey = Voyage (a trip) | Day = Journée (the time)

items.questionText: "The professor's ___ on Cameroonian history was very interesting."
items.feedback: Correct! A 'lecture' is an academic talk by a professor (un cours magistral or conférence). 'Lecture' in French means 'reading' (the activity). Example: 'I like reading' = 'J'aime la lecture'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: academic talk by a professor
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I did a lot of lecture' when you mean 'reading'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Lecture = Cours magistral (Professor's talk) | Reading = Lecture

items.questionText: "Can you send me your ___ on WhatsApp? I want to know where you are."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Location' in English means 'a place' or 'position' (endroit/emplacement). 'Location' in French means 'rental' (renting a car or house). Example: 'This is a good location for a shop' (place).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a place or position
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am looking for a location' when you mean 'a rental apartment'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Location = Endroit/Emplacement (a place) | Rental = Location

items.questionText: "A wedding is a very happy ___. Everyone dresses up."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Occasion' in English means 'a special event' (événement). 'Occasion' in French often means 'second-hand' or 'a bargain'. Example: 'J'ai acheté cette voiture d'occasion' = 'I bought this car second-hand'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a special event or particular time
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I bought this for a good occasion' when you mean 'for a good price'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Occasion = Événement (an event) | Bargain/Second-hand = Occasion

items.questionText: "Please send your ___ and cover letter to apply for this job."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Resume' (or résumé) in English means a CV for job applications. 'Résumer' in French is a verb meaning 'to summarize', and 'un résumé' means 'a summary'. Use 'summary' for book summaries.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to summarize (verb); un résumé = a summary
falseCognate.englishMeaning: a CV (for job applications)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The teacher asked for a resume of the book' when you mean 'summary'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Resume (CV) = CV (for a job) | Summary = Résumé (short version)

items.questionText: "I am going to ___ at my friend's house for the weekend."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Rester' in French means 'to stay' or 'to remain'. 'Rest' in English means 'to relax' or 'sleep' (se reposer). Example: 'You are sick; you need to rest' (relax), but 'I will stay at home' (remain).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to relax, sleep, or take a break
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am going to rest at my friend's house' when you mean 'stay'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Rest = Se reposer (to relax) | Stay = Rester (to remain)

items.questionText: "If you work hard and study well, you will ___ in your exams."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Succeed' in English means 'to be successful' (réussir). 'Succéder' in French means 'to follow' or 'to come after'. Example: 'The Prince will succeed the King' (follow in sequence), but 'I hope you succeed' (be successful).

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to follow, to come after (in a sequence)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to be successful, to achieve a goal
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The sunshine succeeded the rain' when you mean 'followed'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Succeed = Réussir (to be successful) | Follow = Succéder

items.questionText: "My parents ___ my decision to study medicine at the university."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Support' in English means 'to help' or 'to encourage' (soutenir/aider). 'Supporter' in French means 'to tolerate' or 'to endure' something bad. Example: 'Je ne peux pas supporter ce bruit' = 'I cannot tolerate this noise'.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to tolerate, to endure, to put up with
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to help, to assist, to encourage
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I cannot support my neighbor' when you mean 'tolerate'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Support = Soutenir/Aider (to help) | Tolerate = Supporter (to endure)

items.questionText: "When I failed my exam, my teacher was very ___ and gave me encouragement."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Sympathetic' in English means 'showing compassion or pity' (compatissant). 'Sympathique' in French means 'nice' or 'friendly'. Example: 'Your friend is very nice' = 'Ton ami est très sympathique'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: showing compassion or pity for suffering
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'My boss is very sympathetic' when you mean 'nice'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Sympathetic = Compatissant (showing pity) | Nice = Sympathique

items.questionText: "This actor is very ___; he can do comedy, drama, and action films."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Versatile' in English is positive, meaning 'adaptable' or 'able to do many things' (polyvalent). 'Versatile' in French is negative, meaning 'changeable' or 'fickle' (inconstant). Big difference in meaning!

falseCognate.englishMeaning: adaptable, able to do many things (positive)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'He is too versatile' when you mean 'unstable' or 'fickle'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Versatile (English) = Polyvalent (Positive) | Versatile (French) = Inconstant (Negative)

items.questionText: "That manager is cruel; he ___ his employees by shouting at them."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Abuse' in English is a strong, negative word meaning 'to harm' or 'to mistreat' (maltraiter). 'Abuser de' in French means 'to take advantage of' or 'to overuse'. Example: 'You are wasting my time' not 'abusing my time'.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to overuse, to exploit, to take advantage of
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to misuse, to harm, to treat cruelly
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'You are abusing my time' when you mean 'wasting'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Abuse = Maltraiter/Nuire (to harm) | Take advantage = Abuser de

items.questionText: "She worked hard to ___ her goal of becoming a doctor."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Achieve' means 'to accomplish' or 'succeed in doing' something (réussir/accomplir). 'Achever' in French means 'to finish' or 'to complete'. Example: 'I finished my homework' not 'I achieved my homework'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: to accomplish, to succeed in doing something
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I achieved my homework' when you mean 'finished'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Achieve = Réussir/Accomplir (to accomplish) | Finish = Achever

items.questionText: "The photo looks good, but the ___ room is very small."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Actual' in English means 'real' or 'true' (réel/vrai). 'Actuel' in French means 'current' or 'present-day'. Example: 'What is your current address?' not 'actual address' (unless emphasizing it's the real one).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: real or true (not imaginary)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'What is your actual address?' when you mean 'current'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Actual = Réel/Vrai (Real) | Current = Actuel (Present)

items.questionText: "I have a lot of ___ to do at the office today."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Affaire' in French means 'business', 'deal', or 'things to do'. 'Affair' in English most commonly means a secret romantic relationship (liaison). Use 'work', 'business', or 'things' instead.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a secret romantic relationship (cheating)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I have many affairs to do' when you mean 'tasks' or 'work'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Affair = Liaison (secret relationship) | Business/Things = Affaires

items.questionText: "What is the first item on the ___ for today's meeting?"
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Agenda' in English means a list of topics for a meeting (ordre du jour). 'Agenda' in French means a diary or planner (for appointments). Example: 'I need to check my planner' not 'my agenda'.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: a diary, planner, or appointment book
falseCognate.englishMeaning: a list of topics to discuss at a meeting
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I need to check my agenda' when you mean 'planner' or 'diary'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Agenda = Ordre du jour (meeting list) | Planner/Diary = Agenda

items.questionText: "Please don't ___ with me about this decision. It is final."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Argue' in English commonly means 'to disagree angrily' (se disputer). 'Arguer' in French is formal, meaning 'to claim' or 'to make a point'. Use 'make the point that' for formal arguments.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to claim, to argue a point (formal)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to disagree angrily, to fight with words
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I would like to argue that' when you mean 'make the point that'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Argue = Se disputer (disagree angrily) | Claim = Arguer (formal)

items.questionText: "I used my phone's ___ to take a photo of the sunset."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Camera' in English is general, but most often means a photo camera (appareil photo). 'Caméra' in French specifically means a video camera (for moving pictures). Specify 'video camera' for filming.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: photo camera (for still pictures)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Confusing photo camera with video camera
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Camera = Appareil photo (for photos) | Video camera = Caméra

items.questionText: "I am late ___ the traffic was very bad this morning."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Car' in French is a conjunction meaning 'because'. 'Car' in English is a noun meaning 'automobile' (voiture). Use 'because' for the conjunction, not 'car'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: an automobile (voiture)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am late car the traffic was bad' instead of 'because'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Car = Voiture (automobile) | Because = Car/Parce que

items.questionText: "I keep my tools in the ___ under the house."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Cave' in French means 'cellar' or 'basement' (under a house). 'Cave' in English means a large natural underground chamber (une grotte) in mountains. Use 'basement' or 'cellar' for under houses.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: large natural underground chamber (grotte)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'in the cave' when you mean 'in the basement'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Cave = Grotte (natural, in mountain) | Cellar/Basement = Cave

items.questionText: "Please take a ___ and make yourself comfortable."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Chair' in English means a piece of furniture to sit on (une chaise). 'Chaire' in French means a pulpit (in church) or professorship (at university). This is a common confusion!

falseCognate.englishMeaning: piece of furniture to sit on (chaise)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Confusing furniture with professorship
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Chair = Chaise (furniture) | Professorship = Chaire

items.questionText: "In the USA, students go to ___ after finishing high school."
items.feedback: Correct! 'College' in English (especially American English) means 'university' (higher education). 'Collège' in French means 'middle school' (ages 11-15). Example: 'I finished middle school when I was 15'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: university (higher education after secondary school)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I finished college at 15' when you mean 'middle school'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: College (English) = Université | Collège (French) = Middle School

items.questionText: "I am ready to ___ my food now. Can I see the menu?"
items.feedback: Perfect! Use 'order' for food in restaurants (commander). 'Command' is a strong verb meaning 'to give an order' in military or official contexts (donner un ordre). 'Order' is for food, 'command' is for authority.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to order (food in restaurant or goods)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to give an order (military/official, strong)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am ready to command my food' instead of 'order'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Command = Donner un ordre (strong order) | Order = Commander (food/goods)

items.questionText: "I cannot enter the bus; it is ___."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Complet' in French means 'full' (no more space). 'Complete' in English means 'finished' or 'having all parts' (fini/achevé). Example: 'My homework is complete' (finished), but 'The bus is full'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: finished or having all parts
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The bus is complete' when you mean 'full'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Complete = Fini/Achevé (finished) | Full = Complet/Plein

items.questionText: "You must be ___ with your studies and work hard every day."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Consistent' in English means 'regular' or 'steady' (régulier/constant). 'Consistant' in French means 'thick' or 'solid' for food (épais). Example: 'This sauce is very thick' not 'consistent'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: regular, steady, or unchanging
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The fufu is very consistent' when you mean 'thick'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Consistent = Régulier/Constant (steady) | Thick = Consistant/Épais

items.questionText: "What is the ___ for submitting this project? I need to know when to finish."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Délai' in French means 'deadline' or 'time limit' (date limite). 'Delay' in English means 'postponement' or 'something being late' (retard). Example: 'I'm sorry for the delay' (being late).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: postponement or being late
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'What is the delay for this project?' when you mean 'deadline'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Delay = Retard (late) | Deadline = Délai/Date limite

items.questionText: "Can you ___ this package to my office tomorrow?"
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Deliver' means 'to bring or hand over' goods (livrer). 'Délivrer' in French means 'to set free', 'to liberate', or 'to issue' a document. Example: 'The government issued my ID card' not 'delivered'.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: to set free, to liberate, or to issue (document)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: to bring or hand over goods
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The government delivered my ID' when you mean 'issued'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Deliver = Livrer (bring goods) | Issue/Set free = Délivrer

items.questionText: "The football match had a ___ ending in the last minute with a surprise goal!"
items.feedback: Correct! 'Dramatic' in English means 'exciting' or 'sudden and surprising' (spectaculaire). 'Dramatique' in French means 'tragic' or 'very sad' (tragique). Example: 'It was a tragic accident' not 'dramatic accident'.

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: tragic or related to tragedy (very sad)
falseCognate.englishMeaning: exciting, theatrical, or sudden and surprising
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'His death was dramatic' when you mean 'tragic'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Dramatic = Spectaculaire/Soudain (exciting) | Tragic = Dramatique

items.questionText: "I cannot talk right now, I am ___ with an important task."
items.feedback: Perfect! Use 'busy' for 'occupé'. 'Engaged' in English most commonly means 'promised to be married' (fiancé). 'Engagé' in French means 'committed' to a cause or 'hired'. Avoid 'engaged' for 'busy' to prevent confusion!

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: committed (to a cause), hired, or involved
falseCognate.englishMeaning: promised to be married, or busy/occupied
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am engaged' when you mean 'busy' (sounds like marriage!)
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Engaged = Fiancé (to be married) | Busy = Occupé | Committed = Engagé

items.questionText: "We must prepare for a ___ power cut tomorrow. It might happen."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Éventuel' in French means 'possible' or 'potential'. 'Eventual' in English means 'final' or 'ultimate' (happening at the end). Example: 'The eventual winner was from Bamenda' (the final winner).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: final or ultimate (at the end of a process)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'an eventual problem' when you mean 'a possible problem'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Eventual = Final (at the end) | Possible = Éventuel

items.questionText: "In our science class today, we did an ___ with chemicals."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Expérience' in French can mean 'experience' OR 'experiment'. In English, they're different words! Use 'experiment' for scientific tests and 'experience' for life knowledge. Example: 'Visiting Waza Park was an amazing experience'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: knowledge or skill from doing something
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'We did an experience' when you mean 'experiment'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Experience = Expérience vécue (life) | Experiment = Expérience scientifique

items.questionText: "I am sick with a bad cough. I need to see a ___."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Physician' in English means 'medical doctor' (médecin). 'Physicien' in French means 'physicist' (a scientist who studies physics). Example: 'Albert Einstein was a great physicist'. Use 'doctor' to avoid confusion!

falseCognate.englishMeaning: medical doctor (médecin)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Confusing medical doctor with physics scientist
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Physician = Médecin (Medical Doctor) | Physicist = Physicien

items.questionText: "I have a sharp ___ in my back. It hurts a lot."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Pain' in English means 'suffering' or 'hurt' (douleur). 'Pain' in French means 'bread'. Example: 'I am going to buy some bread' = 'Je vais acheter du pain'. Very different meanings!

falseCognate.englishMeaning: suffering or the feeling of being hurt (douleur)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I'm going to buy some pain' when you mean 'bread'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Pain (English) = Douleur (Hurt) | Pain (French) = Bread

items.questionText: "I am sick. I need to see a ___ to get treatment."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Médecin' in French means 'doctor' (the person). 'Medicine' in English means 'medication' or 'drug' (le médicament). Example: 'Take this medicine three times a day' (the drug), not 'see a medicine'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a drug or medication (le médicament)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I need to see a medicine' when you mean 'doctor'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Medicine = Médicament (The drug) | Doctor = Médecin (The person)

items.questionText: "The doctor gave me ___ for my headache."
items.feedback: Excellent! Use 'medicine' or 'medication' for médicament. 'Drug' can mean medicine, but also illegal drugs. 'Drogue' in French almost always means illegal drugs. Say 'medicine' to be clear and avoid confusion!

falseCognate.englishMeaning: medicine/medication OR illegal drugs
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'The doctor gave me drugs' (sounds like illegal substances)
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Drug (English) = Médicament OR Drogue | Drogue (French) = Illegal | Use 'medicine' for médicament

items.questionText: "This food contains no artificial ___ to keep it fresh."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Preservative' in English means a food chemical (conservateur). 'Préservatif' in French means 'condom'. This is a very embarrassing false cognate! Always say 'preservatives' for food, never 'préservatifs'.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: chemical added to food to keep it fresh (conservateur)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Very embarrassing confusion between food chemicals and condoms!
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Preservative = Conservateur (Food chemical) | Condom = Préservatif

items.questionText: "I am waiting in the ___ for the bus at the motor park."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'File' in French means 'line' or 'queue' of people. 'File' in English means 'a folder' (dossier) or 'computer file' (fichier). Example: 'Please save the file on your USB' (document), but 'waiting in line' (queue).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: folder for documents (dossier) or computer file (fichier)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'waiting in the file' when you mean 'line' or 'queue'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: File = Dossier/Fichier (Document) | Line/Queue = File (People waiting)

items.questionText: "I studied hard and got a good ___ in mathematics this term."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Note' in French means 'grade' or 'mark' in school. 'Note' in English means a short piece of writing (un mot). Example: 'The teacher wrote a note to my parents' (message), but 'I got a good grade' (school result).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: short piece of writing (un mot) or to write down
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I got a good note' when you mean 'grade' or 'mark'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Note = Mot/Billet (A message) | Grade/Mark = Note (School result)

items.questionText: "He is in court for his criminal ___."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Procès' in French means a court 'trial'. 'Process' in English means a 'method' or 'series of steps' (processus/méthode). Example: 'Sending mobile money is a simple process' (method), but 'trial' for court cases.

falseCognate.englishMeaning: method or series of steps
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'He is in court for his process' when you mean 'trial'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Process = Processus/Méthode (A method) | Trial = Procès (In court)

items.questionText: "Please ___ the meeting on your phone so we can listen to it later."
items.feedback: Perfect! 'Record' (verb: re-CORD) means 'to write down' or 'to film/audio record' (enregistrer). 'Record' (noun: RE-cord) means a sports achievement OR a file of information. 'Record' in French means sports record. Use 'record' (verb) for filming!

falseCognate.frenchMeaning: record in sports or best achievement
falseCognate.englishMeaning: a file of information OR to write down/film (enregistrer)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Confusing the verb 'to record' with sports records
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Record (noun) = Dossier/Enregistrement | Record (verb) = Enregistrer | Record (achievement) = Record (same!)

items.questionText: "Please fill out this registration ___ and return it to the office."
items.feedback: Excellent! 'Form' in English means 'a paper to fill out' (formulaire) or 'a type/kind'. 'Forme' in French means 'shape' or 'physical fitness'. Example: 'I am not in good shape today' (fitness), but 'fill out this form' (paper).

falseCognate.englishMeaning: a type/kind or a paper to fill out (formulaire)
falseCognate.commonMistake: Saying 'I am not in good form' when you mean 'shape' or 'fitness'
falseCognate.memoryTrick: Form = Formulaire (A paper) | Shape/Fitness = Forme (Physical condition)
